steps: Raise your dominant hand to your forehead, palm facing out, fingers together pointing up.
Move your hand away from your forehead in a small salute-like motion.
tip: A crisp, friendly salute — the standard ASL greeting.

steps: Raise your open hand, palm facing out.
Wave it side to side.
tip: The everyday wave works in ASL too.

steps: Sign GOOD: touch your chin with flat fingertips, then bring your hand down into your other open palm.
Sign MORNING: rest your dominant fingertips in the crook of your other arm (held across your chest), then lift them upward like a sunrise.
tip: Two signs in sequence: GOOD, then MORNING.

steps: Sign GOOD: touch your chin with flat fingertips, then bring your hand down into your other open palm.
Sign NIGHT: rest your dominant fingertips in the crook of your other arm, then move your hand downward over the arm like the sun setting.
tip: Same first sign as GOOD MORNING — only the second sign changes.

steps: Touch your chin with the fingertips of your flat hand, palm facing you.
Move your hand forward and slightly down, ending with your palm angled upward.
tip: Starts at the chin or mouth — as if sending gratitude forward.

steps: Place your flat dominant hand on your chest, palm down.
Rub it in a small clockwise circle.
tip: A flat hand circling the heart.

steps: Make a loose fist, palm facing your chest.
Rub it in small circles over your heart.
tip: A fist making circles. The classic beginner mix-up is PLEASE (flat hand) vs SORRY (fist).

steps: Hold your open hand at your chest, fingers together.
Brush your fingertips upward against your chest twice.
tip: Fingertips brush UP for EXCUSE-ME; a fist circles for SORRY — different signs.

steps: Make a fist with your thumb across your fingers.
Nod it up and down like a head nodding yes.
tip: Pair it with a real nod of your head — natural and expected.

steps: Extend your index and middle fingers, other fingers tucked.
Tap the two fingertips against your thumb once or twice.
tip: Blends the fingerspelled N and O. Always pair with a side-to-side head shake.

steps: Make a fist with your dominant hand and rest it on your other open palm.
Lift both hands upward together.
tip: To offer help to someone, lift the hands toward them.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat, palm up.
Bring your dominant flat hand down sharply onto the palm, like a karate chop.
tip: Sharp and clear — urgency is in the movement.

steps: Point both index fingers forward.
Move both hands forward together.
tip: Point and push away for GO; beckon toward yourself for COME.

steps: Point your dominant index finger toward the person.
Curl it toward yourself in a beckoning motion.
tip: One finger beckoning you closer.

steps: Hold both hands in loose claws in front of you, palms up.
Pull them toward your chest.
tip: As if pulling what you want toward yourself.

steps: Make the letter X: a fist with a hooked index finger.
Bend your wrist downward.
tip: The hooked X handshape bends at the wrist. Do not confuse with ASK, which starts as a straight pointing finger.

steps: Point your middle finger and thumb back toward your chest (not touching).
Move your hand forward while bringing your index finger and thumb together.
tip: Means 'to enjoy'. For 'similar to', use the sign SAME instead.

steps: Touch the fingertips of your flat hand to the side of your forehead.
Move them slightly outward.
tip: Knowledge comes from the head.

steps: Touch your forehead with your flat hand.
Flick your hand outward away from your head while shaking your head slightly.
tip: The flick-away adds the 'not' to KNOW.

steps: Hold your index finger up beside your temple.
Flick it upward sharply.
tip: The flick looks like a light bulb switching on.

steps: Sign UNDERSTAND: flick your index finger up beside your temple.
Shake your head at the same time.
tip: A head shake turns UNDERSTAND into DON'T UNDERSTAND.

steps: Hold your open hand up, fingers together.
Touch your thumb to your chin.
tip: Female signs are located at the chin; male signs at the forehead.

steps: Hold your open hand up, fingers together.
Touch your thumb to your forehead.
tip: Male signs are located at the forehead; female signs at the chin.

steps: Cross your arms as if cradling a baby.
Rock them gently side to side.
tip: Mime rocking an infant.

steps: Hook your two index fingers together.
Reverse them so the other finger ends up on top.
tip: Interlocked fingers — a friendship link.

steps: Form a C with your dominant hand at the side of your forehead.
Hold it there as if tipping the brim of a baseball cap.
tip: From tipping a cap.

steps: Touch your thumb to your cheek near your ear.
Trace it down along your jawline to your chin.
tip: Traces the line of a bonnet strap.

steps: Bring your bunched fingertips to your mouth.
Repeat once or twice, as if putting food in your mouth.
tip: Also means FOOD — context tells which.

steps: Form a C with your hand as if holding a cup.
Bring it to your mouth and tilt it back slightly.
tip: Mime taking a sip.

steps: Form a W: index, middle, and ring fingers up.
Tap the index-finger side of your hand against your chin twice.
tip: The W handshape taps the chin.

steps: Hold your open hand at your chest, fingers pointing down.
Drag it downward toward your stomach.
tip: The hand travels toward an empty stomach.

steps: Point your index finger at your throat.
Trace it downward.
tip: Traces a dry throat.

steps: Bring the fingertips of both hands together in front of you.
Tap them together once or twice.
tip: Asking for another round — fingertips meet.

steps: Hold both hands up, palms facing you.
Flip them outward so the palms face away — 'all done!'
tip: Also marks past tense: FINISHED EAT means 'already ate'.

steps: Hold your flat hand at your chest, palm facing in.
Brush it upward firmly once or twice.
tip: Happy feelings rise upward.

steps: Hold both open hands in front of your face, palms in.
Drag them downward.
tip: The downward movement mirrors a long face.

steps: Hold a claw hand near your face.
Pull it outward sharply.
tip: Sharp, tense movement matches the emotion.

steps: Rest your fingertips on your shoulders.
Let your hands drop, fingers drooping.
tip: Your hands visibly run out of energy.

steps: Touch the tip of your middle finger to the middle of your forehead.
Tap once or twice.
tip: Not feeling well starts at the head.

steps: Point your two index fingers toward each other.
Twist them in opposite directions.
tip: Point toward where it hurts while signing.

steps: Hold two fists at your chest.
Snap them open suddenly.
tip: The sudden opening shows a startled flinch.

steps: Cross both arms over your chest.
Rest each fist on the opposite shoulder in a self-hug.
tip: A hug for yourself.

steps: Hold one arm horizontally across your chest.
Rest your other hand's fingertips in the crook of that arm, then lift them upward in an arc — like the sun rising.
tip: The sunrise arc over a steady horizon.

steps: Hold one arm horizontally across your chest.
Rest your other hand's fingertips in the crook of that arm, then move your hand downward over the arm — like the sun setting.
tip: The sunset arc — mirror image of MORNING.

steps: Hold both flat hands in front of you, palms down.
Drop them down a short distance.
tip: Settles firmly in the present moment.

steps: Point to your wrist with your dominant index finger.
Tap it once or twice, as if tapping a watch.
tip: From checking a wristwatch.

steps: Hold both open hands up, palms facing up.
Give a small shrug-like shake.
tip: In ASL the question word usually comes LAST: YOUR NAME WHAT? Pair it with furrowed eyebrows.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out, palm up.
Tap the fingertips of your bent dominant hand twice on the inside of your wrist.
tip: From a doctor checking your pulse. An older initialized variant taps a D handshape instead.

steps: With your dominant index and middle fingers, draw a small cross on your upper arm.
tip: From the cross on a medic's sleeve.

steps: Make the letter T: a fist with your thumb poking up between your index and middle fingers.
Shake it side to side twice.
tip: The T handshape shakes twice.

steps: Extend your thumb and pinky (the Y handshape).
Hold it to the side of your head like a phone receiver.
tip: The classic call-me shape.

steps: Hold both hands in front of you as if gripping a steering wheel.
Turn them slightly.
tip: Also means DRIVE — context tells which.

steps: Touch your fingertips together to form a roof peak.
Move both hands down and outward to form the walls.
tip: Draws the outline of a house: roof, then walls.

steps: Clap your dominant open hand down onto your non-dominant open palm.
tip: Like a teacher clapping hands for attention.

steps: Raise your thumb, index finger, and pinky together; curl the other fingers.
Hold the hand up proudly.
tip: The iconic ILY handshape combines the letters I, L, and Y.

steps: Sign WHAT: a palms-up shrug.
Point an open palm toward the person (YOUR).
Sign NAME: tap your dominant index and middle fingers across the same two fingers of your other hand.
tip: ASL word order puts the question last: YOUR NAME WHAT?

steps: Sign HAPPY: brush your flat hand upward at your chest.
Sign BIRTHDAY: touch your middle fingertip to your chin, then to your chest.
tip: Two signs in sequence: HAPPY, then BIRTHDAY.

steps: Make both hands into squished O handshapes, fingertips pinching together.
Hold the two O handshapes in front of your chest at shoulder width.
Touch the fingertips together, pull apart, twist the wrists, then touch them together again.
Keep your palms facing each other throughout the whole movement.
Lean in slightly and nod once so it reads as a definite number, not counting.
tip: The twist between the two touches is the signature of NUMBER — tapping alone just looks like counting.

steps: Make both hands into flat open hands, fingers together.
Press your palms together in front of your chest, fingertips pointing forward.
Open the hands outward twice, like swinging a book's covers open.
Keep your palms facing each other as the hands open.
Use the double motion for the noun BOOK; a single opening means OPEN-BOOK.
tip: Two openings = the book itself; reverse the motion to mean CLOSE-BOOK.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up, like a page.
Form a V with the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand, fingertips pinched together like two eyeballs.
Sweep the V fingertips down across the palm, from wrist toward fingers.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while the fingertips glide.
A single sweep means READ; repeat the sweep to mean READING.
tip: The V's fingertips are 'eyes' scanning the page — mime them reading each line of text.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an H, index and middle fingers extended together.
Hold the H handshape in front of your chest, palm facing your non-dominant side.
Move the hand straight down twice in place, with a slightly extended wrist.
Keep both downward taps even and centered; do not drift sideways.
Hold a neutral expression — drifting to the side can read as HARD-OF-HEARING.
tip: Two taps straight down — drifting sideways on the second tap changes the meaning entirely.

steps: Shape both hands into loose C handshapes, fingers curved.
Hold them in front of your chest with the palms facing each other.
Move both hands in a circle so the two C hands come together in the middle.
Finish with the hands nearly touching, palms still facing each other.
Keep the sweep smooth and symmetrical, like students gathering in a room.
tip: An initialized sign: swap the C for an F and you get FAMILY, for a G you get GROUP.

steps: Shape both hands into loose flat hands, palms facing down.
Hold your non-dominant hand steady as a base in front of your chest.
Circle your dominant hand once, then slap it down onto the base hand.
Keep both palms facing down as the dominant hand lands.
Let the hand bounce back up after the slap — freezing on the base reads wrong.
tip: The same sign covers UNIVERSITY; use a U handshape on the dominant hand to mean it specifically.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up.
Pinch your dominant fingertips and thumb together just above the palm.
Lift the pinched fingers up toward your forehead, as if grabbing information.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while you lift.
Aim for the forehead itself, not the top of the head, to keep it LEARN and not TEACH.
tip: Mnemonic: take knowledge off the page and put it into your head.

steps: Make both hands into fists with the thumbs pointing straight up, like little beakers.
Hold your non-dominant fist steady in front of your chest.
Tip your dominant fist over it, as if pouring liquid from a test tube into the beaker.
Keep both thumbs pointing up through the pour.
Pair it with a curious, inquisitive expression — science is about wondering.
tip: Picture pouring chemicals from a test tube into a beaker — the A hands are the lab glassware.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an L, index finger up and thumb out.
Hold the L handshape in front of your chest.
Draw a full circle in the air with the L handshape.
Trace the circle clockwise from your own point of view if you are right-handed.
Keep your face relaxed; mirror the direction if your local signers circle the other way.
tip: An initialized sign — one circling L is all it takes to name the place.

steps: Extend the index fingers of both hands, other fingers tucked.
Bend each index finger into an X hook while your hands move downward.
Trace a question mark in the air, then open both hands into palm-down fives to dot it.
Keep the movement centered in front of your chest.
Use this formal two-handed version for exams; casual quizzes are often just fingerspelled.
tip: Think of drawing a question mark in the air, then dotting it with your open palms.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up, like an open book.
Point the fingers of your dominant hand down at the palm.
Wiggle your dominant fingers as you hover over the page.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while the fingers flutter.
Lean your head in a little to show concentration — STUDY is an active sign.
tip: Wiggling fingers over an open palm: you are poring over the page.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up, and keep it low.
Pinch your dominant fingertips together over the palm and lift them toward your head.
Open both hands into flat palms facing inward.
Move both flat hands straight down past your torso to finish the PERSON ending.
Keep the non-dominant hand down — lifting it toward the head would read as TEACHER.
tip: STUDENT is LEARN plus the PERSON ending; the casual version can look like tossing a paper aside.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up.
Bring your dominant flat hand down on top of it, palm to palm.
Strike the palm twice with a quick repeated backward bounce.
Keep your non-dominant hand perfectly still — only the dominant hand moves.
Two clean strikes is enough; extra hits make it look like you are fanning yourself.
tip: The same two-beat rhythm as a judge stamping documents onto a desk.

steps: Hold up the index finger of your dominant hand, other fingers tucked.
Raise it in front of your chest, palm facing sideways.
Draw a question mark in the air: curve down, then finish with a quick X-hook dot.
Keep the curve and the dot in one smooth flowing motion.
Pair it with raised eyebrows and a slight forward lean — the classic questioning face.
tip: Curve like a hook, then dot — it is literally a question mark drawn in the air.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm up, as your paper.
Pinch your dominant index fingertip against the dip of your thumb, like holding a pen.
Scribble a quick side-to-side motion across the palm.
Keep your dominant palm angled sideways while the pen hand moves.
One careful stroke means writing something specific, like your name; quick repeats mean writing in general.
tip: Think of a pen tip gliding across a page — the movement stays quick and small.

steps: Hold your non-dominant index finger up in front of your chest.
Shape your dominant hand into a G, index finger pointing sideways.
Touch the dominant G fingertip to the side of the non-dominant index finger.
Angle both palms inward toward each other.
Hold the touch for a beat so the word 'lands' before you move on.
tip: A G for 'word' tapping the side of a finger — one pointed little tap.

steps: Touch your dominant index fingertip to your lips.
Hold your non-dominant index finger upright in front of your chest.
Move both hands forward and slightly down together.
Close both hands into loose fists as they travel forward.
Finish with the fists facing each other at chest height, as if delivering a reply.
tip: The same motion also means RESPOND or REPLY; use a stern face to turn it into ORDER or COMMAND.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up.
Shape your dominant hand into a G, index and thumb pinched together.
Tap the G hand down onto the palm twice, bouncing down, up, then down again.
Point the dominant index finger toward your non-dominant side as you tap.
Two taps is the standard rhythm; more taps make it look like you are counting.
tip: This is the school-level version ('what grade are you in?'); a separate variant is used for a letter grade on a paper.

steps: Shape both hands into flattened O handshapes, fingertips touching thumbs.
Hold both hands up near your forehead.
Move both hands forward about six inches.
Change both hands into flat palms facing inward.
Sweep both flat hands straight down past your torso to finish the PERSON ending.
tip: TEACH plus the PERSON ending — take information from your head and put it into someone else's.

steps: Point the index and middle fingers of both hands straight down, like little legs.
Hold the hands in front of your chest, palms facing inward.
Roll both hands forward in alternating circles, like pedaling a bicycle forward.
Keep the circles even and in place — do not travel sideways.
Keep your face relaxed and open; the pedaling rhythm carries the plural meaning.
tip: Two pairs of pointing fingers 'pedaling' forward in the air = a crowd of people.

steps: Shape both hands into F handshapes, thumb and index pinched into circles.
Hold your non-dominant F hand steady in front of your chest.
Circle your dominant F hand forward around it, tracing a dinner-table circle.
Bring both F hands together so the fingertips touch.
Keep the circle smooth — a jerky trace can read as a different group sign.
tip: F hands circling like a family gathered around a table — CLASS and TEAM use the same circle with different handshapes.

steps: Open your dominant hand with the fingers together pointing up.
Touch your thumb to your forehead, palm facing left.
Bring the hand straight down to your chest.
Finish with the thumb touching your chest, fingers still pointing up.
Keep the motion smooth and centered — starting at the chin instead would mean WOMAN.
tip: Same start as FATHER at the forehead, then carried down to the chest for MAN.

steps: Hold both hands in flat open handshapes, fingers together.
Raise them to the sides of your torso, palms facing inward.
Move both hands straight down past your body.
Keep the palms facing each other through the whole drop.
Hold a neutral face — PERSON is the plain citation form for an individual.
tip: Flat hands dropping at your sides: 'one who does.' Add it after a verb to make an agent, like TEACHER.

steps: Hold your dominant hand open with your palm facing down at chest height.
Pat downward once in the air, as if patting the head of a small child.
Shift your hand a few inches to the side and pat downward once more for a second child.
Keep your palm facing down through both pats and keep the motion light.
Use a warm, gentle expression — you are indicating small children, not scolding them.
tip: Two quick pats for two imaginary children; the two-handed version is more formal, for stage or presentations.

steps: Open your dominant hand into a 5, with your thumb sticking out to the side.
Touch the tip of your thumb to your chin, fingers pointing upward.
Bring the hand straight down until your thumb-tip rests on the center of your chest.
Keep your palm angled toward your face through the short downward slide.
Hold a neutral, respectful expression — this is the everyday adult-female sign.
tip: Chin first, then chest: female signs live on the lower half of the face, male signs on the forehead.

steps: Hold your non-dominant forearm horizontally in front of you, as if cradling a baby.
Shape your dominant hand into a flat B, with the palm facing toward your left.
Touch the edge of the dominant hand to your forehead like a salute, marking the male part.
Sweep the dominant hand down into the crook of your non-dominant elbow, ending palm up.
Keep the cradled arm still — do not rock it side to side, that extra movement belongs to BABY.
tip: A compound of MALE plus BABY: salute the forehead, then land in the cradled arm.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a loose C, as if about to cup something small.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your chest with its palm facing up.
Start the C-hand at your chin to mark the female part of the compound.
Glide the C-hand down from your chin and settle it into the upturned palm.
Close the C gently around the lower hand, like two hands joining in marriage.
tip: The efficient everyday version: a C-hand slides from the chin into the waiting palm; a longer GIRL-plus-BELIEVE version also exists.

steps: Hold both hands open with fingers spread and thumbs sticking out to the sides.
Touch both thumb-tips to your forehead, marking the father part of the compound.
Slide both hands straight down until the thumb-tips touch your chin for the mother part.
Keep your palms angled toward each other and your fingers relaxed through the slide.
Pair the slide with a small nod — you are naming a respected relationship.
tip: A compound of FATHER plus MOTHER: one smooth slide from forehead to chin covers both.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a flattened O, fingertips pinched together and facing you.
Bring your fingertips up to your mouth, as if placing a bite of food inside.
Tap your mouth twice with a small, repeated movement.
Keep your fingers relaxed and your wrist loose; the motion stays small and quick.
Nod slightly, as if enjoying the taste — eating is a pleasant sign.
tip: FOOD and EAT share this exact sign — the double tap leans toward the noun, a single tap toward the verb.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a fist and bend your index finger into an X handshape.
Press the bent knuckle of your index finger firmly against your cheek.
Pivot your wrist to twist the knuckle back and forth on your cheek.
Keep your palm facing sideways and your elbow steady so only the wrist turns.
Imagine biting into a crisp apple — the twist mimics the chewing motion.
tip: Twist the knuckle on the cheek; sliding the hand across the face is a different sign.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an R by crossing your middle finger over your index finger.
Touch the R-hand to one corner of your chin.
Move the hand across to touch the other corner of your chin.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your face through the short side-to-side move.
Use the same neutral expression as the EAT family — you are naming a place to eat.
tip: Same mouth-corner path as the eating signs, but with an R handshape marking the word restaurant.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, as if wrapping your fingers around a cup.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with its palm facing up.
Set the C-hand down into the upturned palm, like placing a cup on a saucer.
Add a very small repeated up-and-down motion — keep it tiny, not a big bounce.
Keep your expression neutral; you are showing an object, not drinking from it.
tip: Keep the C-hand level — tipping it toward your mouth turns the sign into DRINK.

steps: Close both hands into S fists, with your thumbs resting against the curled fingers.
Stack your dominant fist on top of your non-dominant fist in front of your chest.
Hold the bottom fist completely still, like the base of an old coffee grinder.
Turn the top fist in small circles, as if cranking the grinder's handle.
Keep your palms facing down and add a focused look — grinding takes effort.
tip: Think of a hand-cranked coffee grinder: the top hand works, the bottom hand anchors.

steps: Hold your dominant hand up near your side, shaped like a modified D.
Snap your middle finger against the base of your thumb, landing in a G-like shape.
Repeat the snap a second time in the same spot.
Keep your palm facing forward and make the snaps small and crisp.
Some signers pat their thigh first — that version is fine, but the snap is the core.
tip: Always snap with the middle finger, never the index — the sign is a lexicalized D-O-G.

steps: Hold both hands up with fingers extended and held straight together.
Touch your fingertips to the center of your chest.
Pivot both hands inward toward each other, then back out, repeating twice.
Keep your fingertips on your chest the whole time — the wrists do the work.
Breathe visibly as you sign, matching the rise and fall of an animal's chest.
tip: The pivoting chest motion imitates breathing — that is the memory hook.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an H: index and middle fingers extended together, other fingers folded.
Hold the H-hand beside your head at temple height.
Bend the two fingers forward twice, like a horse's ears flicking.
Keep your palm facing forward and your elbow relaxed at your side.
Sign with one hand only — skilled signers do not use two hands for HORSE in conversation.
tip: The two fingers are the horse's ears flicking — and one hand is enough.

steps: Hold your dominant hand out to the side with fingers together and palm facing sideways.
Keep your wrist loose and your arm extended at a comfortable height.
Wave your hand side to side while gliding it forward a few inches.
Let the hand trail like a fish's tail — the wiggle comes from the wrist, not the elbow.
Keep a calm, smooth expression to match the gliding swim.
tip: This is the noun 'a fish'; the casting-a-fishing-rod version means the verb 'fishing'.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an open F: thumb and index nearly touching, other fingers spread.
Hold the open F near the corner of your mouth.
Pull the hand outward to the side while closing the thumb and index into a full F.
Keep the outward pull short, about an inch or two, tracing the whisker line.
Imagine stroking a cat's whiskers — keep your face soft and playful.
tip: The closing fingers trace a cat's whiskers — never rub the fingertips together.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with its palm facing down.
Lay your dominant flat hand on the back of it, palm down.
Stroke forward along the back of the hand twice, like petting an animal's back.
Keep your dominant fingers together and make the strokes long and gentle.
Soften your expression — done gently, the sign doubles as the verb 'to pet'.
tip: Gentle strokes mean 'pet'; done extra carefully it reads as petting softly.

steps: Point your dominant index finger with your other fingers curled into a fist.
Place the fingertip at one side of your forehead, just above the eyebrow.
Draw the fingertip straight across your forehead to the other side.
Keep your palm facing down and make the motion smooth in one pass.
Hold a neutral expression — the face stays out of this color sign.
tip: One clean swipe across the brow — that single pass is the whole sign.

steps: Hold your dominant hand open and flat with your thumb extended and fingers together.
Place the open hand against the center of your chest.
Pull the hand straight out away from your chest.
As you pull out, bring your thumb in to touch your fingertips, closing the hand.
Keep your palm facing your chest at the start and your expression neutral.
tip: The closing hand 'collects' the whiteness off your chest as it pulls away.

steps: Point your dominant index finger with the rest of the hand closed into a fist.
Bring the fingertip to the center of your lips.
Stroke downward across your lips one time.
Keep your palm facing you and make the motion short and deliberate.
Some signers touch the chin instead — the lips are the classic location.
tip: One stroke on the lips with a plain index finger — not the initialized R version.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a B: fingers extended together, thumb folded across the palm.
Hold the B-hand out in front of your shoulder, pointing toward your conversation partner.
Twist your wrist side to side in a small shake, like shivering 'brr'.
Keep the shake in the wrist — the elbow stays still and the motion stays compact.
Match it with a slight shiver in your shoulders to sell the 'cold blue' feeling.
tip: Think shivering in the cold — the B-hand trembles like you are chilly.

steps: Hold your dominant hand open with all five fingers spread.
Bring the open hand up in front of your mouth and chin.
Flutter your fingers up and down in a quick wiggle.
Keep your palm facing you and make the fluttering motion small and lively.
Raise your eyebrows slightly, as if asking about or showing off colors.
tip: The wiggling fingers are like a painter's brush dabbing at many colors.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a G: thumb and index pinched sideways, other fingers folded.
Hold the G-hand out in front of your shoulder toward your conversation partner.
Shake the hand from the wrist with a small side-to-side twist.
Let the shake drift slightly to your dominant side as you sign.
Keep the wrist loose and the movement quick — a lazy wrist muddies the sign.
tip: G for green, shaken from the wrist — never from the elbow.

steps: Hold your dominant hand open in a 5, with your middle finger aimed at your earlobe.
Bring the open hand up beside your ear, as if pointing at a gold earring.
Pull the hand downward, closing it into a Y handshape with thumb and pinky out.
Twist the Y once or twice as you pull it down past your cheek.
Keep the motion close to your cheek and finish with the Y pointing downward.
tip: It began as pointing at a gold earring, then signing YELLOW — now it is one fluid pull; context also lets it mean California, 'the Golden State'.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a Y: thumb and pinky extended, middle fingers folded.
Hold the Y out in front of your shoulder toward your conversation partner.
Shake the hand from the wrist with a small side-to-side twist.
Let the shake drift slightly to your dominant side as you sign.
Keep the wrist loose — a stiff shake blurs the Y shape.
tip: Y for yellow, shaken from the wrist — the twin of GREEN with a different letter.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a B: fingers extended together, thumb folded in.
Place the B-hand at the side of your face near your temple, index finger close to the cheek.
Drag the hand straight down along your cheek in one smooth pull.
Keep your palm facing to the side and your fingers together through the drag.
Hold a neutral expression — brown lives on the cheek, not in the face.
tip: The cheek-drag is what separates BROWN from BLUE — location matters.

steps: Form your dominant hand into a K handshape, with the middle finger poking up between the index finger and thumb.
Bring the fingertip of your raised middle finger to the center of your closed lips.
Drag the middle fingertip straight down across your lips in a short stroke, then repeat it once.
Keep your palm facing back toward your own face through both strokes.
Hold a neutral, relaxed face so the color sign stays clear and unhurried.
tip: PINK is an initialized RED: think of the letter P brushing the lips.

steps: Bend the middle finger of your dominant hand forward at the large knuckle, keeping the other fingers relaxed.
Place the bent middle fingertip against the center of your chest, slightly toward your dominant side.
Stroke the fingertip upward along your chest in one smooth motion, then repeat the stroke.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your chest for the whole movement.
Match your face to the feeling you mean, since this sign carries emotional meaning.
tip: Stroke twice for emotions; the rising middle finger is like feelings welling up from the chest.

steps: Hold both hands in front of you as bent B-hands, fingers together and slightly curled.
Position your hands at chest height, one slightly above and in front of the other.
Roll both hands forward around each other in a smooth alternating rotation.
End with your dominant palm resting flat on the back of your non-dominant hand.
Soften your eyes and expression to match the gentle meaning of the sign.
tip: The hands roll kindly around each other like gentle waves; finishing with one hand resting on the other seals the meaning.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing up.
Place your dominant flat hand on top so the palms touch, fingertips pointing across.
Brush your dominant fingertips across the lower palm in one smooth stroke from heel to fingertips.
Keep the dominant palm facing down against the other palm through the whole stroke.
Use a single confident stroke with a pleasant expression to mean NICE.
tip: One wipe across the palm means NICE; wiping twice turns it into CLEAN. A single motion keeps the meanings apart.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a U, with the index and middle fingers extended together.
Hold your non-dominant hand in a fist at chest height as a steady base.
Bring the U-hand down so the fingers rest on the back or side of the base fist.
Turn the U-hand's palm sideways so the fingers point down onto the base hand.
Keep your body still and your expression neutral; this is a plain action verb.
tip: Think of the U-hand as a tool landing on the base fist. You may drop the base hand and circle the U twice in the air instead.

steps: Make a V with your dominant hand, extending your index and middle fingers together.
Start with the fingertips just below your eyes, pointing forward.
Move the V-hand straight outward away from your face toward what you see.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your own face during the movement.
Aim your eyes in the same direction as the movement to show what you are looking at.
tip: The two fingers are your eyes sending their gaze outward. Do not confuse it with LOOK, which points the palm out.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of you as loose open claws, fingers spread and slightly bent.
Start with your hands at arm's length, away from your torso.
Pull both hands back toward your body while closing each hand into a fist.
Turn your palms to face each other as your fists land near your chest.
Add a small nod or satisfied look, as if you have just received something.
tip: The open claws grab and close as they come in — picture snatching something out of the air and keeping it.

steps: Touch the tip of your dominant thumb to the tip of your index finger, making a flattened O.
Hold the hand at chest level, a few inches in front of your torso.
Make a quick small lifting motion, as if you are picking up the thing you just spotted.
Keep your palm facing down through the whole quick movement.
Brighten your face with a look of discovery, like your search just ended.
tip: Lifeprint teaches this as 'discover, pick-up' — the little lift is the moment of finding.

steps: Close both hands into fists and hold them at chest height.
Rest the wrist of your dominant fist on top of your non-dominant wrist.
Tap the dominant wrist down onto the other wrist two or three times.
Keep both palms facing down with the knuckles pointing forward.
Hold your body upright and steady, matching the effort the sign suggests.
tip: The tapping fists look like hard labor at a workbench. Twice or thrice is enough — more taps do not change the meaning.

steps: Touch your dominant thumb to your fingertips to make a flattened O handshape.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up.
Set the flattened O onto the open palm, then slide it forward and off the hand.
Keep the moving hand's palm angled down as it brushes along and leaves the base palm.
Face the direction of the seller, since the forward motion shows money changing hands.
tip: Picture handing coins across a counter: the O lands on the palm and slides forward to pay.

steps: Close both hands into fists and hold them together in front of your chest.
Stack the fists so the dominant one sits on top of the non-dominant one.
Twist both wrists at the same time, as if you are screwing two parts together.
Keep both palms facing inward toward each other during the twist.
Add a focused, purposeful expression, as if you are building something.
tip: Both hands twist together for MAKE. If only the top hand turns, you are signing COFFEE instead.

steps: Extend your dominant index and middle fingers and curve them slightly, like a bent V.
Hold the hand out in front of your chest in neutral space.
Move the hand in a smooth semi-circular arc, swinging right, up, and around to the left.
Angle your palm half downward and half outward through the arc.
Look along the path of the movement, as if watching your journey unfold.
tip: The curved fingers trace a little journey through the air. One smooth circle means traveling around; widen it to show a longer trip.

steps: Open your dominant hand wide with all five fingers spread.
Reach the open hand out toward the person or object you are taking from.
Close your fingers into a fist while pulling your hand back toward your body.
Turn your palm to face yourself as the fist arrives at your chest.
Keep your expression firm and clear so the direction of the action reads plainly.
tip: TAKE is the mirror of GIVE: the hand grabs out there and brings the thing back to you.

steps: Hold both hands flat in front of you with the fingertips together and palms facing forward.
Start with the hands touching or nearly touching at chest height.
Swing both hands apart and slightly toward yourself, as if opening double doors.
End with the hands apart and your palms turned to face back toward you.
Keep your movements smooth and your face open and expectant.
tip: The sign copies real life: two flat doors swinging open. For a gift, angle the palms a little more downward at the start.

steps: Point the index finger of your dominant hand straight up.
Touch the side of your forehead with the tip of your index finger.
Hold the touch briefly, or circle the fingertip in a tiny motion on the forehead.
Keep your palm facing back toward your own head.
Look thoughtful, with your gaze slightly raised, to match the meaning.
tip: The index finger points at the brain. Keep it on the forehead; dropping it to the chin turns it into a different sign.

steps: Make a Y with your dominant hand, extending your thumb and pinky while folding the middle fingers.
Hold the Y beside your head, near your ear and mouth, like an old telephone receiver.
Push the Y-hand outward away from your head by a few inches.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your face during the short push.
Keep your face neutral; the meaning is a general phone call, not a specific person.
tip: The Y is the classic telephone handset. Aim it outward for a voice call; aim it at a person to show who you called.

steps: Form a V with your dominant hand, index and middle fingers extended and together.
Hold the V-hand out in front of your face at eye level.
Move the hand deliberately toward whatever you are actively watching or examining.
Keep your palm facing outward, away from your face, for the whole sign.
Move your eyes with the hand and look alert, as if you are really searching.
tip: SEE is passive with the palm in; LOOK is active with the palm out. The palm-out V is the one that goes browsing.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the fingers together.
Point your dominant index finger at the spot where the other hand's index and middle fingers meet.
Give the dominant index finger a small twisting turn, as if turning a key.
Keep the twisting finger's palm facing sideways during the turn.
Start your sentence with an alert, ready expression that matches a new beginning.
tip: Think of turning an ignition key between the two fingers. The twist is small — a big twist looks like a different sign.

steps: Make Y handshapes with both hands, thumbs and pinkies extended.
Hold both Y-hands in front of your chest, a few inches apart.
Twist both wrists back and forth in a playful alternating shake.
Keep the palms facing toward each other through the whole shake.
Smile and look lively, since PLAY always carries a fun feeling.
tip: Two shaking Y-hands look like pure fun. Keep the twist in the wrists, not the elbows.

steps: Touch your dominant thumb to your fingertips to form a flattened O.
Start with the hand close to your own body at chest height.
Move the hand outward in a straight line toward the person receiving.
Angle your palm slightly upward as the hand travels outward.
Look toward the recipient so the direction of giving is unmistakable.
tip: GIVE points at its receiver: move it toward them to give to them, toward yourself to show receiving.

steps: Bend the fingers of both hands at the base joints and touch the thumb to the finger pads, like flattened O shapes.
Hold both hands close to your body at chest height.
Push both hands straight forward away from your body in one smooth motion.
Keep both palms angled slightly down as the hands move forward.
Face your imaginary customer with a businesslike, open expression.
tip: SELL is BUY in reverse: BUY brings money in, SELL pushes goods out. Do not sign it one-handed.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing up.
Touch the tip of your dominant index finger to the center of the open palm.
Flick the index finger forward off the palm toward the person being paid.
Keep the moving finger's palm facing sideways during the flick.
Aim the flick at the recipient and keep your expression matter-of-fact.
tip: The fingertip taps the palm like a coin landing, then flies to the payee. Aim it — PAY is directional.

steps: Make L handshapes with both hands, extending the index finger and thumb.
Hook your dominant thumb around your non-dominant index finger to link the hands.
Wiggle both index fingers alternately while pushing both hands forward together.
Keep both palms facing down so the wiggling fingers read as legs.
Move with energy and lean slightly forward, as if you are really sprinting.
tip: The two index fingers are legs pumping. Faster, bigger wiggles mean a faster run — the sign shows speed.

steps: Close both hands into A or S fists, thumbs lying alongside the fingers.
Hold both fists in front of your torso, close to your body.
Arc both hands forward and upward in one determined pushing motion.
Bend your wrists as you move so your palms face forward at the finish.
Keep a determined, effortful expression to show you are genuinely attempting.
tip: The T-handshape version is Signed English, not ASL — stick with A or S fists for TRY.

steps: Point your dominant index finger forward, other fingers tucked away.
Start with the fingertip resting near your chin.
Move the hand forward in a short arc, as if flipping a word off your chin.
Aim the motion at the person being told; pull toward yourself for TELL-ME.
Keep a straightforward, conversational expression while signing.
tip: TELL is directional — aim it at whoever receives the message, or at yourself to mean TELL-ME.

steps: Shape both hands into flat B hands, fingers straight and together.
Hold the hands upright in front of you, palms facing each other like two doors.
Swing both hands inward together until the fingertips meet in the middle.
Keep the palms facing each other through the whole shutting motion.
Use a firm, definite expression — CLOSE is a firm, finished statement.
tip: One hand shutting means CLOSE-DOOR specifically; both hands shutting means CLOSE in the general sense.

steps: Close both hands into S fists, thumbs across the fingers, like gripping a steering wheel.
Hold both fists in front of your chest at wheel height.
Move both hands in alternating forward-and-back motions, as if steering.
Keep your palms angled toward each other, thumbs resting on top.
Make the motion larger and directional for DRIVE; a small repeated bounce means the noun CAR.
tip: Small repeated bounce = CAR (the noun); larger traveling movement = DRIVE (the verb).

steps: Point your dominant index finger toward the person you are asking.
Hold the hand at chest height, aimed squarely at them.
Bend the index finger into an X hook while the hand moves toward them.
Keep your palm angled toward the person being asked.
Pair it with raised eyebrows and a questioning lean — ASK is a question sign.
tip: The index-finger-to-X change is the asking motion — and ASK is directional, so aim it at the person.

steps: Hold up your dominant hand in a four handshape, all four fingers extended.
Hold the hand near your mouth, index finger closest to your chin.
Move the hand backward twice, tapping the index finger just below your lower lip each time.
Keep your palm angled back toward yourself through both taps.
Use a conversational, animated expression while the fingers 'speak'.
tip: The index finger 'speaks' off the chin — two backward taps, not one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand like a small telescope: thumb up, index finger extended, other fingers folded.
Hold the hand beside your eye, aimed outward at what you are watching.
Fix the aim steady and keep it pointed at the event.
Keep your palm facing sideways, thumb resting on top.
Fix your gaze in the same direction — your eyes and hand point together like a spectator.
tip: WATCH is for spectator events like TV, movies, and sports; use LOOK-at for studying something up close.

steps: Pinch your dominant index fingertip against your thumb, like picking something up.
Hold the pinched fingers out in front of you at chest height.
Grab your 'choice' from the air and pull the hand up and toward yourself.
Keep your palm facing down as you pull the choice in.
Nod slightly as you finish — choosing is a decisive act.
tip: Pluck your favorite option out of an imaginary lineup and keep it for yourself.

steps: Shape both hands into loose A handshapes, thumbs sticking out.
Hold your non-dominant A hand steady in front of your chest.
Touch the thumb of your dominant A hand to your forehead, then bring it down to tap your other thumb.
Keep both thumbs pointing up through the whole movement.
Use a thoughtful, knowing expression — the thought starts in your head.
tip: The A hand 'stores' the thought at the forehead, then anchors it down onto the other hand.

steps: Start with your dominant index finger touching your forehead — the THINK part.
Hold your non-dominant hand out in front of you, palm facing up.
Bring the dominant hand down and cup it over the non-dominant hand, as if marrying the thought.
Let the dominant hand open into a loose C handshape as it lands.
Keep a sincere, steady expression — belief is held, not questioned.
tip: BELIEVE is a THINK + MARRY compound: thoughts you have 'married' become your beliefs.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, fingers curved and thumb out.
Hold the C hand at the top of your chest.
Slide the hand straight down the middle of your chest in one single motion.
Keep your palm facing your body as it travels downward.
Use a soft, longing expression — the wish comes from your heart.
tip: Same handshape as HUNGRY, but WISH uses one slow downward stroke instead of a repeated bounce.

steps: Shape both hands into flat B hands, fingers together and straight.
Hold them in front of your chest at a comfortable distance.
Push both hands forward in the direction you want to show movement.
Keep both palms facing the direction of the push.
Aim your gaze along the movement — the direction is part of the meaning.
tip: MOVE is directional: push toward where the thing is going — forward, up, sideways, or back.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand in an S fist, steady in front of your body.
Start your dominant hand as a loose open claw, fingers spread wide.
Sweep the dominant hand inward toward your body, closing it into an S fist as it goes.
Lift the closed fist upward, finishing above your non-dominant hand.
Finish with a proud, triumphant expression.
tip: Imagine snatching the prize out of your other hand and lifting it high — that arc is the win.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a V, index and middle fingers extended.
Hold the V hand in front of you at chest height.
Open and close the two fingers twice, like scissors snipping.
Keep your palm angled sideways while the fingers snip.
Keep a focused expression — the snip is sharp and deliberate.
tip: The V fingers are scissors; cutting with a knife uses a flat hand instead — CUT depends on the tool.

steps: Shape both hands into flat B hands, fingers together and straight.
Hold them out in front of you, palms facing up like carrying a tray.
Pull both hands toward your body in one smooth motion.
Keep both palms facing up as the hands travel inward.
Angle your body slightly toward the destination — BRING is directional.
tip: BRING aims at its destination: pull toward yourself for BRING-to-me, aim outward for BRING-to-someone.

steps: Shape both hands into loose fists, as if gripping a small stick.
Hold both fists together in front of your chest, side by side.
Twist both hands apart sharply, as if snapping the stick into two pieces.
End with the fists separated and angled outward from each other.
Use a sudden, decisive expression — the snap happens all at once.
tip: This is the physical 'snap-apart' version; a rest or holiday break uses VACATION instead.

steps: Point the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand straight down in a V, like little legs.
Hold the V hand above your non-dominant flat palm, which is the dance floor.
Glide the V fingers side to side across the palm, bouncing lightly like dancing feet.
Keep the V palm facing down toward the floor hand.
Smile and sway a little — DANCE carries a joyful rhythm.
tip: The V fingers are legs gliding across the floor — picture feet dancing.

steps: Point the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand straight down in a V, like legs.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up, as the ground.
Set the V fingertips down onto the palm and hold them still, standing upright.
Keep the V fingers pointing straight down, palm facing sideways.
Hold a tall, upright posture yourself — your body mirrors the sign.
tip: Inverted-V fingers are legs: planting them on the flat palm means standing still.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up.
Lay your dominant flat hand on top of it near the wrist.
Brush the dominant hand across the palm once, toward the fingertips.
Keep your dominant palm facing down as it slides.
One smooth wipe means CLEAN; repeat the wipe to mean CLEAN-up, like brushing a table.
tip: One wipe = the state of being clean; two wipes = the act of cleaning up.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a loose claw, fingers spread and slightly bent.
Hold the hand beside your ear, fingertips pointing toward it.
Bend the fingers gently toward your ear a couple of times, as if gathering sound.
Keep your palm angled toward the side of your head.
Tilt your head slightly toward the hand and focus — you are straining to hear.
tip: The claw fingers 'scoop' sound into the ear — wiggle them to show listening hard.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand in an S fist in front of your chest — the sun.
Shape your dominant hand into a 1, index finger pointing up.
Circle the 1 hand all the way around the fist, like the earth orbiting the sun.
Close the circling hand into an S fist as it completes the orbit.
One full circle equals one year — repeat the circle for multiple years.
tip: One orbit of the earth around the sun = one YEAR; change the starting handshape to count years.

steps: Extend your non-dominant arm in front of you, bent at the elbow, hand pointing to the side.
Rest your dominant elbow on the non-dominant hand, with your dominant hand pointing up.
Lower the dominant hand down and to the side until it rests on your non-dominant forearm near the elbow.
Keep the non-dominant arm perfectly still — only the top hand travels.
Hold a neutral, matter-of-fact expression — DAY is a plain time marker.
tip: Keep the lower arm still like a table; only the upper hand travels down to the elbow.
